answer_plain: In one desert sand sample, hydrogen-eating microbes could fix at most about 0.05 g of carbon per m² per year, if a rain like this fell every two weeks and all the energy from hydrogen went into making cell carbon. The model's estimate of this ceiling ranges from 0.006 to 0.27 g. In a second sample, which lacks the carbon-fixing genes, the ceiling is exactly 0.
answer_science: We bounded CO₂ fixation by H₂-oxidising autotrophs by converting the twin's H₂ uptake with the knallgas yield (0.167 mol CO₂ per mol H₂; Bongers 1970), assuming that all oxidised H₂ supports growth. In sample F14Dr1, the bound after a single 12 mm rain is 1910 µg C m⁻² over 14 days; repeating such a rain every two weeks gives 0.050 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹ (reference parameterisation 0.058 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹; 90 % interval 0.0062 to 0.27 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹), with the H₂ rate constant k_H2 explaining most of the variance (S_T = 0.83). In sample 14PRr2 the reasoner entails no H₂-autotroph candidate, and the bound is zero by deduction.

limits_plain: The range shows how much the answer moves when uncertain numbers in the models are varied; the models themselves could also be wrong. This figure is an upper ceiling, not measured net carbon storage in the sand, because microbes also burn energy just to stay alive and release carbon dioxide when they respire.
limits_science: The bound assumes that all energy from H₂ oxidation goes into growth; atmospheric H₂ oxidisers use much of it for persistence (Jordaan et al. 2020), so realised fixation lies below the bound. Net carbon removal requires measured stock changes.
